newsitem.title: BOSNIA: UN sees spring 1997 return of enclave to Croatia.
newsitem.headline: UN sees spring 1997 return of enclave to Croatia.

text.p: Croatia and the top U.N. official in the country agreed on Tuesday that a rebel Serb enclave should revert to government rule in the spring of 1997, dismissing hints of a dispute over the timetable.

The U.N. Security Council will make the final ruling before the end of 1996 but is expected to heed the advice of Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. Transitional Administration in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES).

Under a Croatian-Serb accord hammered out on the fringes of the Dayton peace talks on Bosnia last November, UNTAES was authorised to stay for a year with the option of up to one year more if any party sought its presence.
But the Croatian parliament passed a resolution last week demanding that the mandate of the UNTAES mission end in January 1997 as scheduled without an extension sought by local Serb authorities.
Zagreb has been sceptical of suggestions by U.N. officials that UNTAES might need more time to safeguard Serb minority rights, fearing the process could drag on indefinitely.
But the Croatian minister overseeing Eastern Slavonia's "reintegration" and Klein said on Tuesday they had concurred on the general timing for a handover.

"It was agreed that UNTAES completely hand over to Croatian administration in early spring (1997)," Deputy Prime Minister Ivica Kostovic said after he, President Franjo Tudjman and Klein had consultations in Zagreb.
"Croatia wants an early end to the mandate and so do we. This is not an open-ended U.N. mandate," Klein, an American diplomat, told reporters.

"The way I'm looking at it now is (to) work towards an early spring return of the region to Croatian (rule) and then phase out our mandate (by) early summer. So I think our goals are very similar," he said.
Five thousand U.N. combat troops, now securing the enclave along its 1992 ceasefire line after disarming the Serb militia, would leave within three months of the mandate's expiry.
Kostovic, asked by reporters if Croatia could accept a restoration of Croatian control in April 1997, implying a three-month extension of the U.N. mandate, replied: "Yes."

Tudjman, in a statement later, said Eastern Slavonia must be returned "on schedule". He cited "immense pressure" from 80,000 Croat war refugees to regain their homes not to mention "the entire Croatian public and parliament".
"Croatian preferences have varied with the assumption of the international community that more time may be needed to guarantee Serb rights," a senior Western diplomat said.
"The issue isn't settled yet. But I think there's more commonality than differences on the duration of UNTAES."

Analysts say prospects for an orderly handover of Eastern Slavonia have brightened following a normalisation treaty between Croatia and rump Yugoslavia and Zagreb's broadening of a war amnesty for Serb rebels.
Minority Serbs took up arms and captured three large swathes of Croatia in a 1991 war against its move to independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia.
The Croatian army reconquered two of the Serb enclaves in blitz attacks across U.N. truce lines last year.
U.S. envoys then brokered a peaceful solution for Eastern Slavonia to avert another Croatian offensive that would have jeopardised the new peace process in nearby Bosnia.

UNTAES entered Eastern Slavonia last January and has since demilitarised the fertile Danube River enclave, created a joint Serb-Croat police force and restored telephone and postal links across truce lines to prepare for reintegration.
